\subsection*{(c) PBE (10 marks)}

Let $\mu(H|N)\in[0,1]$ denote Uni's posterior belief that Peter is type $H$ given he submitted $N$ papers. Uni accepts iff its expected payoff is non-negative: $\mu(H|N)\cdot1+(1-\mu(H|N))\cdot(-1)=2\mu(H|N)-1\geq0\iff\mu(H|N)\geq0.5$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Peter's dominant strategy.} Peter's acceptance payoff is $5-2N$ (Type H) and $5-3N$ (Type L). Whether Uni accepts or rejects, $N=0$ gives Peter a strictly higher payoff than $N=1$ and $N=2$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
N & \text{H accepts} & \text{H rejects} & \text{H comparison} \\ \hline
0 & 5 & 0 & \text{benchmark} \\
1 & 3 & 0 & 3<5 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & 1<5
\end{array}
\]
For Type H: $5>3>1$, so $N=0$ strictly dominates $N=1$ and $N=2$ regardless of Uni's action.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
N & \text{L accepts} & \text{L rejects} & \text{L comparison} \\ \hline
0 & 5 & 0 & \text{benchmark} \\
1 & 2 & 0 & 2<5 \\
2 & -1 & 0 & -1<5
\end{array}
\]
For Type L: $5>2>-1$, so $N=0$ strictly dominates $N=1$ and $N=2$ regardless of Uni's action.

Since $N=0$ strictly dominates $N=1$ and $N=2$ for both types, in any PBE Peter plays $N=0$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Uni best-responds at the on-path node $N=0$.} Both types play $N=0$, so $\mu(H|0)=0.2<0.5$. Accepting at $N=0$ gives expected payoff $0.2(1)+0.8(-1)=-0.6<0$, so Uni strictly prefers to reject. Peter's equilibrium payoff is $5$ (acceptance, given Uni rejects).

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Off-path beliefs (sequential rationality).} Consider what Uni would do at off-path nodes if they were ever reached.

\textbf{At $N=1$:} If Peter were to deviate to $N=1$, only Type H would do so (Type L gets $5>2$ at equilibrium vs $2>0$ from acceptance at $N=1$). By the intuitive criterion, $\mu(H|1)=1$. Accepting gives $2(1)-1=1>0$, so Uni would accept.

\textbf{At $N=2$:} Only Type H would deviate to $N=2$ (Type L gets $5>-1$ at equilibrium vs $-1<0$ from acceptance at $N=2$). By the intuitive criterion, $\mu(H|2)=1$. Accepting gives $2(1)-1=1>0$, so Uni would accept.

Uni has no profitable deviation at any node; Peter has no profitable deviation. All incentive constraints are satisfied.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 4 — Separating equilibria are impossible.} Because $N=0$ strictly dominates $N=1$ and $N=2$ for both types, neither type has any incentive to deviate from $N=0$. Any candidate separating profile (e.g., $N_H=1,N_L=0$) fails: Type L would deviate to $N=0$ (gets $5>2$), and Type H has no reason to deviate away from $N=0$ either. No separating PBE exists.

\bigskip
\[
\boxed{\text{PBE: Peter plays } N=0 \text{ (both types); Uni rejects at } N=0,\ A\text{ at } N=1,2.}
\]

\textbf{Can Uni learn?} No. Both types play the same signal $N=0$ regardless of type, so Uni cannot update her belief. Uni cannot learn Peter's type.

\subsection*{(c) PBE via backward induction (10 marks)}

\bigskip
\textbf{Setup:} We let $s_P^*(H)$ and $s_P^*(L)$ be Peter's strategy for type $H$ and type $L$, and $s_U^*(N)$ be Uni's strategy after observing $N$. We let $\mu(H|N)=q_N$ be Uni's updated belief that Peter is type $H$ given he chose $N$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — University's optimal strategy (given belief $\mu$).}

Uni observes $N$ and chooses Accept (A) or Reject (R).

Expected payoff of Accept: $q_N \cdot 1 + (1-q_N)\cdot(-1) = 2q_N - 1$.
Expected payoff of Reject: $0$.

Hence:
\[
\boxed{\text{Uni accepts } \Leftrightarrow\ q_N \geq 0.5;\quad \text{Uni rejects } \Leftrightarrow\ q_N < 0.5.}
\]

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Peter's optimal strategy (given Uni's best response).}

We consider each possible Uni's strategy and find Peter's optimal $N$.

\textbf{Case analysis of Uni's strategy:}

\bigskip
\textbf{Case 1: Uni accepts at $N=0$ (i.e., $q_0 \geq 0.5$).}

Then Peter receives payoff $5-2N$ (Type H) and $5-3N$ (Type L). Both types prefer $N=0$ since $5 > 3 > 1$ and $5 > 2 > -1$.

Peter's optimal strategy: $s_P^*(H) = s_P^*(L) = N=0$.

The corresponding belief at $N=0$: Since both types play $N=0$ with probability 1, by Bayes' rule $q_0 = 0.2 < 0.5$. This contradicts the assumption $q_0 \geq 0.5$. Hence \textbf{no PBE} in this case.

\bigskip
\textbf{Case 2: Uni rejects at $N=0$ (i.e., $q_0 < 0.5$).}

Then Peter's payoff at each $N$ (given Uni's action):

\textbf{Type H:} Acceptance payoff $= 5-2N$, Rejection payoff $= 0$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
N & \text{Accept} & \text{Reject} & \text{Best response} \\ \hline
0 & 5 & 0 & \text{Accept} \\
1 & 3 & 0 & \text{Accept} \\
2 & 1 & 0 & \text{Accept}
\end{array}
\]

\textbf{Type L:} Acceptance payoff $= 5-3N$, Rejection payoff $= 0$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
N & \text{Accept} & \text{Reject} & \text{Best response} \\ \hline
0 & 5 & 0 & \text{Accept} \\
1 & 2 & 0 & \text{Accept} \\
2 & -1 & 0 & \text{Reject}
\end{array}
\]

Peter's optimal strategy: $s_P^*(H) = s_P^*(L) = N=0$ (both types prefer $N=0$).

\bigskip
\textbf{Consistency check:} Since both types play $N=0$, by Bayes' rule:
\[
q_0 = \frac{0.2}{0.2+0.8} = 0.2 < 0.5,
\]
which is consistent with Uni's optimality (reject at $N=0$). \checkmark

\bigskip
\textbf{Off-path beliefs:} At $N=1$ and $N=2$, if Peter deviates:
\begin{itemize}
\item At $N=1$: Only Type H would deviate (Type L gets $5 > 2$ at equilibrium vs $2$ from accepting at $N=1$). By the intuitive criterion, $q_1 = 1$. Expected payoff of accepting: $2(1)-1=1>0$, so Uni accepts.
\item At $N=2$: Only Type H would deviate (Type L gets $5 > -1$ at equilibrium vs $-1$ from accepting at $N=2$). By the intuitive criterion, $q_2 = 1$. Expected payoff of accepting: $2(1)-1=1>0$, so Uni accepts.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip
\textbf{Verification of sequential rationality:}

At $N=0$: Both types accept and get $5 > 0$ (rejection). Uni rejects (expected payoff $2(0.2)-1=-0.6<0$). No profitable deviations.

At $N=1$: Uni accepts (payoff $1>0$). Type H gets $3$, Type L would get $2<5$ at equilibrium, so Type L does not deviate.

At $N=2$: Uni accepts (payoff $1>0$). Type H gets $1$, Type L would get $5> -1$ at equilibrium, so Type L does not deviate.

\bigskip
\[
\boxed{\text{PBE: } s_P^*(H) = s_P^*(L) = N=0;\quad s_U^*(0) = R,\ s_U^*(1) = A,\ s_U^*(2) = A.}
\]

\textbf{Can Uni learn?} No. Both types play the same signal $N=0$ in equilibrium, so observing $N=0$ reveals no information about Peter's type. Uni cannot learn Peter's type from his strategy.

$\square$
